entry.title: FP64 Performance and the Limits of Ozaki Emulation on HPC Systems
entry.summary: A growing industry narrative holds that native double precision can be deprioritized in HPC accelerators, on the hypothesis that low-precision tensor cores can emulate FP64 on demand, and that most HPC workloads are bandwidth-bound. This paper evaluates some of those claims and explores the importance of FP64 in scientific computing. We show roofline profiling data of representative HPC workloads, across a variety of common computational motifs, to evaluate the arithmetic-intensity and accuracy requirements of these workloads. We also consider FP64 emulation via the Ozaki method to ascertain some of the possibilities and limitations of these approaches. These results indicate that Ozaki emulation should not be evaluated as a general replacement for FP64, but as an optimization for the subset of workloads whose dominant computation is sufficiently large, dense, and GEMM-shaped. Our analysis indicates this is less than 10\% of the HPC ecosystem. Furthermore, even in this favorable regime, standalone GEMM speedup is not enough to accelerate (or avoid performance regression) for the application: numerical behavior, workspace requirements, matrix shape, and integration overhead determine whether the benefit survives at application scale. This paper characterizes those boundaries empirically. Furthermore, we show that dense GEMM accounts for only a small fraction of FP64 computation across HPC workloads, leaving most application-level FP64 work beyond the reach of GEMM-based emulation.

entry.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
entry.summary: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite broad potential impact of selection bias it is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct selection bias, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle, applicability, limitations and data requirements. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R and prepares input for the external SPREG software. It provides worked examples using simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with open methodological challenges.

entry.title: Multi-phonon wobbling excitations as a probe for dynamical quasiparticle alignment
entry.summary: The multiple and very extended triaxial strongly deformed bands of the $^{163,165}$Lu nuclei are used to ascertain the spin dependence of the odd quasiparticle alignment. The band heads are found to favor a tilted alignment geometry which gradually evolves into a transverse configuration. Distinct dynamical regimes are thus identified in specific bands and spin intervals, which are discussed in terms of wobbling excitations based on the analysis of the wave functions and $E2$ transition probabilities.

entry.title: CARF: Context-Aware Reasoning Supervision for Scientific Evidence Screening
entry.summary: Systematic reviews synthesize biomedical evidence to inform clinical and public-health decision-making, but require domain experts to manually screen thousands of studies against detailed eligibility criteria. We investigate whether language models can assist with this bottleneck by learning from expert feedback on title and abstract screening decisions and model-generated reasoning. We introduce the Context-Aware Reasoning Framework (CARF), a human-in-the-loop framework that uses expert feedback on model-generated reasoning to adapt language models to context-dependent screening tasks. We evaluate CARF on systematic reviews of verbal autopsy and cause-of-death ascertainment methods used in global public health mortality surveillance. CARF shows competitive screening performance compared to evaluated models while retaining high sensitivity, and is more inclined to retain ambiguous, context-dependent studies for human review. Together, these findings suggest that expert-corrected reasoning is a promising supervision signal for context-dependent scientific screening, while retaining a role for human oversight.

entry.title: Capillary forces between two identical spherical particles
entry.summary: The properties of colloidal suspensions and granular matter change drastically upon adding a small amount of liquid capable of forming capillary bridges between the solid particles. The attractive forces exerted by these liquid bridges induce the formation of particle aggregates and networks, which radically changes the macroscopic mechanical and rheological behaviour. Predicting these forces across bridge sizes, particle separations and wettability is therefore central to particle-scale modelling of capillary suspensions and wet granular matter. While the Young-Laplace equation governing the properties of the liquid bridges is well known, it lacks a convenient analytical solution. Current simulations therefore employ approximate analytic expressions, typically developed for contact angles below ~40° and bridge volumes below ~2.5% of the solid particle's volume. We compare several frequently used expressions from the literature with numerical solutions of the theoretical capillary forces. An overall good agreement is observed in the aforementioned parameter ranges, while the approximate expressions start to deviate outside their intended domains. We propose accurate and computationally efficient expressions for the capillary force that model this behaviour, for contact angles from 5° to 80° and bridge volumes from $10^{-6}$ to 0.15. We also explore mesoscopic 'fluid-scale' simulations of bridges by Multi-body Dissipative Particle Dynamics (MDPD), to ascertain whether this coarse-grained fluid model faithfully captures the continuum capillary forces. Remarkably, a good agreement is observed even for liquid bridges described by a mere few dozen fluid particles. Together, these results offer two approaches, at different resolution scales, for simulating bridges over a wide range of bridge volumes and contact angles.

entry.title: Towards optimal selection schedules for online active learning
entry.summary: We consider the problem of online linear classification, where a stream of unlabeled samples is available, and annotation is costly. We investigate the optimal query policy, that prescribes whether and when a sample should be labeled and used for a training step, or instead discarded, so as to minimize a given objective. We focus on the realizable case, under Gaussian design, in the high-dimensional regime where data dimension and number of unlabeled samples grow proportionally. We consider two objectives: 1) the generalization error under a labeling budget, and 2) a cumulative cost function where mistakes have unit cost and queries cost $Δ$. We first show that the myopic policies that greedily minimize at all times the increment in the objective correspond to either small or intermediate-margin policies, that prescribe the selection of samples whose margins fall within certain intervals that shrink with time. Within this class, we numerically ascertain the optimal schedules for the selection thresholds that minimize the final values of the objectives. Taking inspiration from the myopic policy for the cumulative cost, we design a very simple query policy schedule that we compare to other proposed heuristics, on synthetic data and real medical image datasets. Finally, we discuss myopic policies for two-layer neural networks, and exemplify how naive margin-based policies can cease to be optimal.

entry.title: The Magnetized Universe: From planet-forming disks to the high-redshift universe
entry.summary: The interstellar medium (ISM) is magnetized at all scales and phases in our Galaxy and other galaxies across the Universe. Spectro-polarimetric millimetre observations are essential to probe the role of the interstellar magnetic fields in the dynamics of the cold universe, and how this affects the star formation process, and planet formation in nearby star forming regions. Such observations are also essential for understanding magnetic fields in active stars and the shaping and evolution of the circumstellar environments of evolved stars. While ALMA has been revolutionary in advancing our knowledge about magnetic fields in the ISM, the limitations in calibration, especially for circular polarization, and sensitivity for large samples, have hindered robust measurements of field strengths, which are essential for fully assessing their role in ISM dynamics. An ALMA2040 that broadens spectro-polarimetric capabilities to include robust circular calibration and increases sensitivity with more collecting area will enable crucial observations of magnetic fields across the Universe and over a wide range of spatial scales to fully ascertain the influences of magnetic fields from galaxy assembly to forming planets.

entry.title: A Hybrid Gaussian Process-Extreme Gradient Boosting Machine Learning Framework for Robust Knockdown Factor Prediction and Reliability-Based Design of Thin Spherical Shell Caps
entry.summary: Elastic buckling remains a critical concern in the design of deep spherical shell caps, given that experiments reveal a significant reduction of critical loads from those predicted by linearized eigen-buckling analysis. This discrepancy has been attributed to initial geometric imperfections and is often reconciled through a dimensionless parameter, namely the knockdown factor (KDF). However, conventional KDFs (NASA SP-8007; Eurocode 3) are highly conservative, as they represent the lower bound of an extensive body of experimental data. This study aims to narrow the conservatism in the KDFs for spherical shell caps through machine learning (ML) regression models trained on experimental data on spherical shell buckling. A hybrid model is proposed by combining Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and its improved performance is demonstrated over conventional ML algorithms, i.e., the Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Support Vector Regressor (SVR), Random Forest Regressor (RFR), and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (HGBoost). Each of these models uses six input features and a single output, i.e., the KDF. The most critical feature affecting the KDF is ascertained through a sensitivity analysis. The study concludes with a reliability-based design framework that relies on the predictive ML model to obtain safety-consistent, yet less conservative, KDFs.

entry.title: Ascertaining Learning: Generative AI, the Proxy Problem, and Cognitive Competence in University Mathematics
entry.summary: For decades, university mathematics assessed executable procedure, computing and reproducing standard proofs, as a proxy for the understanding it cared about, because procedure was cheap to mark and understanding was not. Generative AI now executes much of this procedure. It does not merely let students bypass the proxy; it exposes how much of what was certified was a proxy. The crisis is not simply cheating but a proxy problem, and resolving it forces a question the discipline has long avoided: what is the irreducible human core of mathematical competence, and how can it be built when some of the executable work can be offloaded? We set out two futures: displacement-and-re-centering, in which AI takes over some execution and education moves toward judgment, formulation and verification; and atrophy, in which premature offloading may erode capacities that depend on prior construction. At the heart of the optimistic future is a verification instability: some forms of oversight are cheap and bounded, while others approach the competence required to construct the work. The outcome is a design choice, not a technological destiny. Rather than add a model, we state the response as two principles: construct before you delegate, and let verification set the ceiling: how far a student can independently verify AI output limits what they may safely delegate. We illustrate with a sequence and two worked problems, and close on the question: whether the construct-before-delegate dependency is a hard constraint or an artefact of how mathematics has been taught.

entry.title: No Convincing Evidence for Tidal Binary Clusters in the Galaxy
entry.summary: Context. The existence of tidal binary clusters (TBCs) in the Milky Way has been repeatedly suggested using Gaia DR3 astrometry and recent catalogs of binary clusters and groups. However, the dynamical feasibility of forming truly bound binary clusters through tidal capture remains uncertain. Aims. We perform a systematic reassessment of twenty star clusters, currently claimed as members of TBCs from the catalog of binary and grouped clusters of Liu et al. (2025) to ascertain their classification. Methods. For each candidate pair, we use Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry to perform a simultaneous and self-consistent opti mization of age, distance modulus, reddening, and metallicity. Results. Our analysis shows that all studied TBCs fail in the required physical condition that ages are compatible with independent formation. After applying strict evolutionary criteria, these systems are more naturally explained as co-eval members of primordial cluster pairs or groups rather than products of tidal capture. Conclusions. We conclude that genuine tidal binary clusters, if present in the Milky Way, must be extremely rare. This work un derscores the importance of robust age determinations and physically motivated selection criteria in future searches for dynamically assembled cluster pairs.

entry.title: Learning Strategies to Break Judges
entry.summary: As AI agents surpass human performance, it becomes exceedingly hard for system designers to evaluate them directly and understand their failure modes. Consequently, agents themselves are being deployed extensively to evaluate, judge, and provide feedback on model traces. But this raises an important question: how can we trust the judge? In this work, we propose an agent-guided method to find weaknesses of agentic judges that expose interpretable failure mechanisms. Our method focuses on mathematical reasoning and proceeds in two stages: first, we deploy adversarial agents to mutate a set of sound proofs by introducing errors, attempting to misguide judges---in other words, injecting errors that judges are unable to catch. Then, we distill these attempts into a small set of mutation strategies which allow us to analyze the failure modes of the judges. To ensure that these strategies are not overfit to the initial set of proofs, we evaluate them by applying the mutation strategies to a held-out set of proofs and querying the same judge. We deploy our method on GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Opus 5, paired with their agent orchestrators, Codex and Claude Code, respectively. These are used both as mutators to introduce errors and as judges to evaluate correctness of mathematical reasoning. We find that across all the agentic judges, we are able to distill mutation strategies that consistently bypass their evaluations, thereby enabling us to ascertain actionable failure modes. Our analysis also reveals that judge reliability degrades at the frontier: errors in Olympiad-level proofs or graduate-level mathematical texts are detected more consistently, whereas flaws in research-level manuscripts are more likely to escape detection.

entry.title: Progression- vs Automata-based Anticipatory Monitoring of LTL over Finite Traces (Extended Version)
entry.summary: When safety-critical systems are developed from a known internal specification, their correctness can be established by model checking. In the frequent case where such a specification is unknown or inaccessible, runtime verification presents an attractive alternative, e.g., to ascertain that autonomous and agentic systems as well as business processes satisfy desirable properties and/or comply with safety requirements. In this paper we study anticipatory monitoring, an advanced form of runtime verification, where the monitoring state is determined by both the trace prefix seen so far, and all its possible finite-length, future continuations. We focus on monitoring linear-time properties that may involve arithmetic constraints. Automata-based approaches, the de-facto standard in this setting, are notorious for their computational complexity. We propose an alternative approach based on progression and LTLf satisfiability checking, for both propositional and arithmetic settings. We experimentally compare the automata- and progression-based approaches, and a third method that combines the two. Our experiments suggest that the progression-based approach often succeeds in producing a verdict when the automata constructions do not terminate, especially for the arithmetic setting. For the propositional setting, the combined technique provides a good tradeoff.

entry.title: Periodic homogenization in scalar Hencky plasticity
entry.summary: This paper investigates the periodic homogenization of a two-phase elasto-plastic material in the framework of $Γ$-convergence. It establishes the link between the homogenized functional and that which was previously obtained in [12] in the context of two-scale convergence. Although there is no gap between the two formulations and that involving two-scale has the hallmark of a (two-scale) elasto-plastic problem, we are unable to positively ascertain the elasto-plastic character of the homogenized energy except in a one-dimensional setting.

entry.title: Improved $B\to K^*_0\left(1430\right)$ transition form factors at next-to-leading order in light cone sum rules
entry.summary: We present an improved determination of the $B\to K_0^*(1430)$ transition form factors using light-cone sum rules (LCSR) with an expansion near the light cone. We include the one-loop radiative corrections to the twist-2 and asymptotic twist-3 distribution amplitudes of the scalar meson and perform the calculation consistently in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme. It allowed us to quantify the impact of radiative corrections on the form factors for each twist. A daughter sum rule is used from the $B\to K_0^*(1430)$ LCSR to ascertain Borel mass and threshold parameter simultaneously. We find that the dominant theoretical uncertainties arise from the $K_0^*(1430)$ distribution amplitudes and its decay constant. Our results are presented in a form that facilitates the incorporation of future improvements in these nonperturbative inputs, including those from lattice QCD and experimental measurements, and can be readily extended to other scalar mesons.

entry.title: Morphology of Solar Filaments During the Solar Maximum of Cycle 24: A Study of 35 Filaments Focusing on Chirality, Barb Orientation, Skewness, and Eruptive Behavior
entry.summary: Filaments in the solar atmosphere are plasma structures held aloft by magnetic fields, counteracting the pull of gravity. Analyzing their magnetic structure is challenging due to the lack of direct observations of their magnetic fields. However, through multi-wavelength intensity observations, one can infer their morphology. We identified 35 solar filaments during the maximum period of the solar cycle 24. In order to ascertain their chirality, we analyzed H$α$ intensity observations. Using coronal ultraviolet intensity images, we also determined the skewness of the related coronal arcades. Furthermore, based on adjacent active regions, we classified filaments as quiescent or active, according to strength of nearby photospheric magnetic fields. We followed every filament over time to estimates their characteristics. The hemispheric chirality preference is followed by 27 (77%) filaments across all categories, based on observed bearing sense. We examined the skewness of the coronal arcades connected to 19 filaments, and they all complied with the hemisphere helicity criterion. The morphology of 16 filaments was also ascertained by integrating the skewness and bearing sense. There were two filaments with sheared arcade morphology and fourteen with flux rope shape. Additionally, by analyzing the changes in the skewness of coronal arcades and the bearing sense of filament barbs over time, we examined the variation in filament magnetic structure. Further, we examine the temporal evolution of selected filaments, which exhibit peculiar characteristics during the observational period. Lastly, we investigated the eruptive characteristics of these filaments. We did not find filaments that are more likely to explode because they do not adhere to the hemispheric chirality preference.
